title: Our Song
description: A banjo-driven debut-era love song where a young couple turns slamming doors, late-night taps and first dates into a song of their own.

pops.text: Taylor wrote this in about 20 minutes for a ninth-grade talent show. She never expected it to end up on an album, let alone become a single.
The inspiration was simple: she and her boyfriend did not have a song. So she went ahead and wrote them one.
Months after the talent show, classmates were still singing the melody back to her in the halls. That was her clue to fight for it on the track list.
She made it the closing track on purpose. The final line asking to 'play it again' was meant to nudge listeners to replay the whole album.
Producer Nathan Chapman built the track around banjo and fiddle, with a fiddle solo in the break. Pure Nashville, teenage edition.
Director Trey Fanjoy shot the video with no single storyline — just front-porch, flower-field and black-and-white performance setups stitched together.
The video premiered on CMT on September 24, 2007. Look for the glitter guitar and the pool of roses Swift lounges in.
At 17, Swift became the youngest person to write alone and sing a No. 1 on Hot Country Songs. It stayed on top for six straight weeks.
It crossed over too, peaking at No. 16 on the Billboard Hot 100 and going four-times platinum in the US.
The clip won both Video of the Year and Female Video of the Year at the 2008 CMT Music Awards.

title: Mine
description: The Speak Now lead single flashes forward from a coffee-shop meet-cute through marriage and kids, as a guarded girl finally lets herself fall in love.

pops.text: Swift wrote 'Mine' in Texas while on the Fearless Tour. It became the opening track on Speak Now.
The song is about her habit of running from love to avoid heartbreak — and imagining what happens if she finally lets her guard down.
She announced it as the lead single on a Ustream live stream on July 20, 2010, weeks before anyone heard it.
A leak forced Big Machine to rush-release it on August 4, about two weeks early. Swift said the leak made her cry.
She produced it with Nathan Chapman at his Pain in the Art studio in Nashville, keeping that country-pop rush of 'Love Story' but for grown-ups.
Rolling Stone singled out one line — about making 'a rebel of a careless man's careful daughter' — calling it a brilliant throwaway detail.
The video was Swift's directorial debut, co-directed with Roman White. The time-jumping story ends with the couple married with two sons.
It was filmed in Kennebunkport, Maine, with the wedding shot at Christ Church on Dane Street. Toby Hemingway plays the groom, cast after Swift saw Feast of Love.
It debuted at No. 3 on the Hot 100 on 297,000 downloads in its first week, topping the digital songs chart.
The video won Video of the Year at the 2011 CMT Music Awards — and former President George H. W. Bush brought his grandchildren to its Maine premiere.

title: Mean
description: A banjo-stomping kiss-off to harsh critics that became an anti-bullying anthem, staged in the video as vaudeville vignettes at a grand old theatre.

pops.text: Swift wrote this for critics who were not offering constructive notes — just attacking everything about a person. Her word for them: mean.
It is the most country-sounding track on Speak Now: banjo-led, with fiddle, mandolin, hand claps and a bluegrass bounce.
That banjo was pointed, too. Swift leaned into it after being told she was not country enough.
Fans first got it October 19, 2010, in the iTunes countdown to Speak Now. Country radio did not get it as a single until March 2011.
The lyrics answer critics who hammered her singing after shaky live TV performances in 2009 and 2010 — flaws she says she already knew about.
Director Declan Whitebloom filmed the video over two days at the Orpheum Theatre in Los Angeles, mixing vaudeville and O Brother, Where Art Thou? touches.
A young Joey King appears in the video, as a girl shut out at lunch for wearing the wrong colour ribbon who ends up applauding in the theatre.
Other vignettes flip too: a bullied fashion-magazine reader becomes a top designer, and a costumed fast-food worker becomes an executive.
It peaked at No. 2 on Hot Country Songs and No. 11 on the Hot 100, then sold over a million US copies by August 2011 — her 13th song to do so.
At the 2012 Grammys it won both Best Country Song and Best Country Solo Performance. Rolling Stone later ranked it among the greatest country songs ever.

title: Back to December
description: A wintry power-ballad apology — Swift alone in a snow-filled house, slipping a letter into her ex's coat as he walks a snowy small town.

pops.text: This was a first for Swift: an apology song. She said the person had been wonderful to her, she dropped the ball, and he deserved to hear it.
She refused to name the subject at the time. Taylor Lautner confirmed in 2016 that the song was about him.
Like every song on Speak Now, she wrote it entirely alone, and produced it with Nathan Chapman.
The sweeping strings were recorded at Capitol Studios in Los Angeles. It is one of only three Speak Now tracks with a full orchestral string section.
As a promo single it debuted at No. 6 on the Hot 100 with 242,000 downloads in its first week — huge for a ballad with no video yet.
French director Yoann Lemoine shot the video in late December 2010, just before Christmas, leaning hard into the cold.
Lemoine said E.T. helped inspire his approach, and he wanted Swift natural and stripped-back — no princess glitter, just snow, distance and sadness.
The snowy exteriors were shot around Binghamton, New York, including MacArthur Park, while Swift's house scenes were filmed outside Nashville. Model Guntars Asmanis plays the ex.
On the Speak Now World Tour she mashed it up live with OneRepublic's 'Apologize' and her own 'You're Not Sorry.'
It peaked at No. 3 on Hot Country Songs and is certified triple platinum in the US.

title: Karma
description: Swift and Ice Spice romp through a cosmic, Easter-egg-packed fantasy — lassoing planets, riding out karma as a cat, a boyfriend and a god.

pops.text: Swift revealed the title on October 6, 2022, in her TikTok Midnights Mayhem series, as track eight from Midnights.
She told Apple Music she wrote it from a happy place — feeling proud of doing things right and trusting that must be a reward.
Producer Sounwave called the beat a last-minute Hail Mary. Jack Antonoff sent it to Swift, and she had her vocals and the song done the next day.
The shimmer comes from cascading synths and Omnichord, blending synth-pop, chillwave, disco and electroclash at a laid-back 90 beats per minute.
Rolling Stone named 'Karma' the fourth-best song of 2022, praising how Antonoff's sleek production meets Swift's wordplay.
On release week it debuted at No. 9 on the Hot 100 — part of the week Swift became the first artist ever to occupy the entire Hot 100 top 10.
Ice Spice's team first reached out about collaborating. Swift called her personally, Ice Spice said yes instantly, and the remix landed May 26, 2023.
Swift directed the video herself and premiered it live at her Eras Tour show in East Rutherford, with Ice Spice as surprise guest, before it hit YouTube the next day.
Spot the Easter eggs: blue nails and the Roman numerals MCMLXXXIX point to 1989, Olivia the cat looms huge, and the final shot is a coffee-cup foam clock striking midnight.
The remix pushed 'Karma' to No. 2 on the Hot 100 — Ice Spice's highest-charting single — and earned a 2024 Grammy nomination for Best Pop Duo/Group Performance.

title: I Can Do It With a Broken Heart
description: Taylor Swift turns heartbreak into a glittering Eras Tour pep talk, smiling through the show in an upbeat anthem from The Tortured Poets Department.

pops.text: Check the track listing: this is track 13 on The Tortured Poets Department, landing on Swift's famous favorite number.
Swift wrote and produced this with Jack Antonoff, pairing some of her saddest lyrics ever with bouncy, shimmering electropop.
The song is about the early Eras Tour, when Swift was hiding depression and heartbreak while performing for stadium crowds every night.
It became the second and final single from the album, sent to radio in July 2024, months after the record dropped.
It debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100 and went on to become the longest-charting song from the whole album in the US.
On tour, the live number is a silent-movie pantomime: her dancers revive a worn-out Swift with tailcoats, feathers and canes straight out of old Hollywood.
Swift directed this video herself, stitching together Eras Tour concert footage and behind-the-scenes rehearsal clips.
Spot the famous cleaning cart: the video finally shows Swift being wheeled to the stage hidden inside it, plus her dive beneath the stage.
Fans saw this video before the internet did: it premiered on the big screens at Wembley Stadium on August 20, 2024, closing the tour's European leg.
USA Today named it the best song of 2024, and its single cover is a freeze-frame of Swift performing it live in Lyon, France.

title: Beat It
description: Michael Jackson's anti-violence rock crossover from Thriller, powered by Eddie Van Halen's guitar solo and a landmark gang-dance video.

pops.text: Quincy Jones pushed Jackson to put a rock song like The Knack's 'My Sharona' on Thriller. Jackson wanted a rock record that school kids and college students alike would buy.
This was Thriller's third single, released on Valentine's Day 1983, right behind 'The Girl Is Mine' and 'Billie Jean.'
Hear that crunch under the solo? It's Toto's Steve Lukather, who played all the rhythm guitar and the bass on this track.
When Quincy Jones first phoned Eddie Van Halen about playing the solo, Van Halen thought it was a prank call and hung up on him.
Van Halen recorded his famous solo completely free, as a favor to Quincy Jones, and took no payment for it.
He didn't just solo and leave: Van Halen rearranged the song's middle section, and a nervous Jackson thanked him for caring enough to make it better.
CBS Records refused to pay for this video, so Jackson financed it himself. It went on to become one of the most celebrated music videos ever made.
Jackson insisted on real Los Angeles gang members, Crips and Bloods, dancing alongside professional dancers and choreographer Michael Peters.
The song spent three weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 and won two Grammys in 1984: Record of the Year and Best Male Rock Vocal Performance.
Forty years on, the video joined YouTube's Billion Views Club in November 2023, Jackson's third clip to reach the milestone.

title: Africa
description: Toto's dreamy soft-rock ode to a continent its writer had never visited, which grew from an album afterthought into a billion-stream phenomenon.

pops.text: That brassy opening riff was born on a new Yamaha CS-80 synthesizer, and David Paich sang the chorus into existence in about ten minutes.
The chorus came fast, but Paich then spent six months polishing the lyrics before he dared show the song to the rest of the band.
Paich had never set foot in Africa. He built the song from a late-night TV documentary, National Geographic, and his schoolteachers' missionary stories.
Geography check: the lyric puts Kilimanjaro rising above the Serengeti, but the mountain is actually more than a hundred miles from it.
This almost never made the album. The band grew tired of it, nearly cut it, and Paich thought about saving it for a solo record.
The groove is a loop before loops were easy: Jeff Porcaro and percussionist Lenny Castro played for five minutes, picked their two best bars, and looped the tape, no click track.
That twinkling kalimba riff was programmed on a Yamaha GS-1 piano, recorded six separate times with different rhythms, and layered together.
Its parent album Toto IV won Album of the Year at the 1983 Grammys, and 'Africa' became Toto's only No. 1 single on the Hot 100.
In 2018 a teenage fan's Twitter campaign talked Weezer into covering it. Their version climbed to No. 51 and dragged the original back onto the charts.
Since 2019, a solar-powered sound installation hidden in the Namib Desert has played this song on an endless loop, meant to outlast us all.

title: Free Fallin'
description: Tom Petty's breezy San Fernando Valley daydream, written almost as a joke with Jeff Lynne and turned into his biggest, longest-charting hit.

pops.text: This started as a joke: Petty sang the first verse just to amuse co-writer Jeff Lynne, who started laughing, then leaned in when the chorus arrived.
Lynne trimmed one chord too many from the riff and told Petty to sing the chorus higher, which is why 'free' stretches out before 'fallin'' lands.
The pair wrote and recorded the song in just two days, making it the very first track finished for Full Moon Fever.
The day after writing it, they cut it at Heartbreaker Mike Campbell's studio, with Lynne himself playing bass and singing backing vocals.
There's no specific girl in this song. Petty said it came from his drives along Ventura Boulevard, name-checking Reseda, Mulholland and the Valley vampires.
It's billed as a solo record, but the Heartbreakers are all over Full Moon Fever, and fellow Traveling Wilburys pitch in across the album.
MCA Records first shelved Full Moon Fever, saying they didn't hear a single on it. New management later released the same record to huge success.
Director Julien Temple shot the video in the Valley world of the lyric, complete with skateboarding from pro skater Mark 'Gator' Rogowski.
It peaked at No. 7 on the Hot 100 in January 1990, Petty's highest- and longest-charting song, and sits on Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Songs list.
Petty played it at the 1989 MTV Video Music Awards with Guns N' Roses' Axl Rose and Izzy Stradlin, and again at the Super Bowl halftime show in 2008.

title: We Don't Talk About Bruno
description: Encanto's gossipy ensemble showstopper, where the whole Madrigal family spills Bruno's secrets in the Disney song nobody was supposed to talk about, and everybody sang.

pops.text: Lin-Manuel Miranda calls this a family gossip song: every verse hands the same chord progression to a different Madrigal, and each one rides it with a totally different rhythm.
Notice who's missing: Bruno himself, voiced by John Leguizamo, doesn't sing a single note in the song all about him.
This clip is the film scene itself, posted to DisneyMusicVEVO on December 29, 2021, and it doubles as the song's official music video.
Under all the gossip sits a Colombian chachacha groove, part of Miranda's plan to root the whole Encanto score in Colombian rhythms.
Nobody pushed this as a single. It topped the Hot 100 in its fifth week with almost no radio airplay, carried entirely by streaming and TikTok.
It held No. 1 for five weeks, becoming only the second song from a Disney animated film ever to top the Hot 100, after Aladdin's 'A Whole New World' in 1993.
That same week, the Encanto soundtrack and this song led the Billboard 200 and Hot 100 together, a soundtrack double last managed by A Star Is Born.
It was never Oscar-nominated for a simple reason: Disney submitted 'Dos Oruguitas' instead, before the film even premiered and anyone knew 'Bruno' would explode.
The Oscars performed it anyway in 2022, its first live performance, with surprise guests including Megan Thee Stallion and Becky G.
It later won the Grammy for Best Song Written for Visual Media, and gave Miranda, its sole writer, his first-ever No. 1 on the Hot 100.

title: Can't Stop the Feeling!
description: Justin Timberlake's sunshine-in-my-pocket anthem from DreamWorks' Trolls, the feel-good smash that debuted at No. 1 and opened the Oscars.

pops.text: This was written for DreamWorks' Trolls — Timberlake voices the grumpy Branch and was the film's executive music producer, overseeing the whole soundtrack.
Timberlake co-wrote it with Swedish hit machines Max Martin and Shellback, the team behind some of the biggest pop smashes of the era.
The song debuted straight in at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 — only the 26th song in chart history to pull that off.
It went on to become the best-selling song of 2016 in the United States, outselling every Drake and Rihanna hit that year.
The official video was directed by Mark Romanek, the visionary behind Michael and Janet Jackson's 'Scream' and Taylor Swift's 'Shake It Off.'
No choreographed pop-star routine here — the video hands the dancing to everyday people busting moves in a diner, a grocery store, a barbershop and a laundromat.
Timberlake performed it live as the interval act at the 2016 Eurovision Song Contest final in Stockholm — a rare American invasion of Europe's biggest pop party.
It won the Grammy for Best Song Written for Visual Media, beating out a field of far moodier movie songs.
Nominated for the Best Original Song Oscar, it opened the 2017 Academy Awards with Timberlake dancing through the Dolby Theatre aisles — then lost to La La Land's 'City of Stars.'
Not everyone was charmed: Time magazine named it the worst song of 2016, calling it impossible to escape. The dancing public disagreed.

title: Julius
description: The horn-blasted, gospel-charged opening track from Hoist, where Phish throws a 15-piece soul party to kick off their most accessible album.

pops.text: This is the opening track of Hoist — and within a minute, the Tower of Power horns announce this will not be a typical Phish record.
Trey Anastasio wrote it with his longtime lyric partner Tom Marshall, but the sound is pure Stax-style soul revue.
That's the Tower of Power horn section — the go-to brass crew of 1970s soul — punching through the choruses.
The Rickey Grundy Chorale supplies the gospel call-and-response, chanting 'don't take another' behind Anastasio's vocal.
Backing singers Rose Stone and Jean McClain bring direct Sly and the Family Stone DNA to the session.
Page McConnell gets to cut loose on organ while producer Paul Fox keeps the whole 15-member ensemble party tight.
Phish debuted it live on April 4, 1994 at Burlington's Flynn Theatre, a week after Hoist came out — with the Giant Country Horns joining in for the occasion.
It was strong enough for network TV: Phish performed 'Julius' on the Late Show with David Letterman in the summer of 1995.
Check the credits — Mike Gordon isn't just on bass here, he's also picking the mandolin.
At 4 minutes 42 seconds, the studio 'Julius' keeps the party compact — a soul single from a band famous for never playing anything the same way twice.

title: Bathtub Gin
description: Phish's tipsy singalong from Lawn Boy — recorded in 1989 on studio time the band won in a battle of the bands, and destined to become one of their most beloved live jam vehicles.

pops.text: The lyrics were co-written by Susannah Goodman with Trey Anastasio — a rare outside lyric credit in a catalog dominated by Tom Marshall.
Phish recorded this in 1989 at Archer Studios in Winooski, Vermont, using studio time they won by taking first place in a Burlington 'Rock Rumble' contest.
It landed on Lawn Boy, released in September 1990 and cut mostly live in the studio with very few overdubs.
Page McConnell opens it with a wild, free-form piano romp, and the studio version sprinkles in sound effects that act almost like a fifth band member.
The surreal lyric tour includes Brett making soup for ambassadors and a sad tale about the kids under the carpet and the purple humpbacked whales.
This track and 'Split Open and Melt' were the two songs Phish cut for Lawn Boy with that prize studio time — not a bad return on a battle-of-the-bands win.
Its other signature reading is the 'Went Gin' from the Great Went festival on August 17, 1997 — the version fan voters put at the very top of the Gin pile.
The song's jam potential first cracked open on August 13, 1993 in Indianapolis, one of the earliest times Phish stretched it into a true improvisational vehicle.
Phish.net has logged more than 320 performances of 'Bathtub Gin' — it grew from a deep cut into a setlist cornerstone.
The studio original clocks in at just 4 minutes 28 seconds — but live, the band happily lets it run five times that long.

title: Ghost
description: The funky title track of The Story of the Ghost — a 3:52 studio miniature that became one of Phish's mightiest live jam vehicles, seen here at Madison Square Garden in 2017.

pops.text: This is the title track and opener of The Story of the Ghost, Phish's deep dive into the loose, danceable sound fans dubbed 'cow funk.'
The album was built backwards: the band held marathon in-studio jam sessions, then mined their favorite improvised moments and wrote songs around them.
'Ghost' premiered live on June 13, 1997 at the S.F.X. Centre in Dublin, Ireland, emerging out of a 'Chalk Dust Torture' jam on a night Phish debuted seven new originals.
Anastasio and Tom Marshall wrote it, and drummer Jon Fishman shares the lead vocal — listen for his voice answering Trey's.
The studio version is a tidy 3 minutes 52 seconds. Live versions generally run 10 to 26 minutes — the song was born to stretch.
Within weeks of its debut it was already exploding: Amsterdam got a 20-minute version on July 1, 1997, and Atlanta's July 23 reading ran nearly 27 minutes of shape-shifting funk.
Many fans crown the Radio City Music Hall 'Ghost' from May 2000 as the definitive version — a slow-building masterclass in group improvisation.
This performance comes from August 5, 2017 at Madison Square Garden, during the Baker's Dozen residency — 'Boston Cream' night, for those keeping donut score at home.
The leftover improvisations from the album sessions were too good to waste: they were later shaped into the ambient instrumental album The Siket Disc.
Phish.net counts more than 220 performances of 'Ghost' — not bad for a song about a friend who never actually speaks a word.

title: Birds of a Feather
description: The Talking Heads-flavored lead single from The Story of the Ghost — a rare full-band writing credit that became Phish's genuine radio hit of 1998.

pops.text: Track two on The Story of the Ghost, this was the album's lead single — released as a promotional single by Elektra in 1998.
It's a true group composition: all four band members share the writing credit alongside lyricist Tom Marshall, a rarity in the Phish catalog.
Hear the Talking Heads in its DNA? The tune channels 'Crosseyed and Painless,' a hangover from Phish's Halloween 1996 performance of Remain in Light.
It premiered on April 2, 1998 at Nassau Coliseum, opening night of the legendary four-show Island Tour.
Just two nights later in Providence, only its second performance ever stretched to 15 minutes — the flock learned to fly fast.
The studio cut adds a proper horn section: Dave Grippo on saxophone, James Harvey on trombone and Jennifer Hartswick on trumpet.
Before the album was even out, the song turned up in the Dawson's Creek episode 'The Kiss' on October 7, 1998 — playing while Pacey steals a police car.
October 1998 was a TV blitz: Farm Aid on CMT, PBS's Sessions at West 54th hosted by David Byrne, and the Late Show with David Letterman on October 27.
It became a real radio hit, peaking at No. 14 on Billboard's Adult Alternative Songs chart in December 1998.
Decades later it surfaced on the MLB The Show 23 video game soundtrack — and modern live versions sometimes open with Page McConnell triggering 'The Birds' samples and a shouted 'They attack!'
